extracted.intended_audience: public relations counsel, press-relations practitioners, journalism/PR students
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for public relations counselors on creating, supplying, and placing news and on ethical and tactical obligations to the public and the press. Covers news value, media selection, event-creation, verification, audience segmentation, and professional standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: News as the newspaper’s backbone / PR must supply and create news
rubrics_metrics.description: Since news is the newspaper’s backbone, the public relations counsel must not only supply news — he must create news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The counsel is 'the purveyor of truthful, accurate and verifiable news' and more logically the 'creator of news.' Examples: arranging events (banquets, launches, demonstrations), staging a shop opening with graphic examples, sending invitations on bricks to create a story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthfulness, accuracy and verifiability
rubrics_metrics.description: Material furnished to the press must be truthful and accurate and verifiable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors are 'suspicious and cynical' but quick to detect falsehood; one spurious error can be fatal to the counsel's relationship with editors. Verify facts as if an editor had assigned a reporter; avoid libelable rumors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness is an important but not exclusive element of news
rubrics_metrics.description: Timeliness ('fresh information of something that has lately taken place') is often required of news but is neither necessary nor sufficient by itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many timely occurrences never become news; timeliness must be paired with other news-value elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty / 'departure from the established order'
rubrics_metrics.description: Mr. Irwin: news is 'a departure from the established order' — events that depart from regularity (crime, exceptional virtue, surprising contrasts) have news value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration: a boiler explosion that leaves a baby carriage undisturbed is more newsworthy than the mere deaths because it 'departs widely' from expectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interest tied to audience preferences ('we prefer to read about the things we like')
rubrics_metrics.description: People prefer news about subjects they like; newspapers often slant coverage by audience (e.g., 'power for the men, affections for the women').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counsel should consider the tastes and typical interests of the target readers and departments when preparing material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Familiarity / recognizability increases interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Interest in news increases in direct ratio to familiarity with the subject, its setting, and its dramatis personae.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use recognizable characters, settings, or recurring institutions to raise the story's appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal impact / effect on readers’ personal concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Interest in news is in direct ratio to its effect on readers' personal concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame stories to show personal relevance or impact to the audience to increase news value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of persons/activities affected
rubrics_metrics.description: Interest increases with the general importance of the persons or activities affected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use prominent spokespeople or showcase influential participants to raise the story's significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overt act / definable manifestation required for news separation
rubrics_metrics.description: Before events become news they usually must make themselves noticeable by some overt act — something definite with unmistakable form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of manifesting acts: bankruptcy filing, fire, collision, arrest, a speech, a vote, a published editorial, a price change or a proposed bridge. PR counsel can create such overt acts (ceremonies, wired appeals, staged demonstrations) to 'uncovers' the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor material to particular newspapers, departments and editors
rubrics_metrics.description: Material must not only have timeliness and interest but must 'suit the particular needs of each particular newspaper and, even more than that, it must suit the needs of the particular editor in whose department it is hoped that it will be published.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different departments (news, editorial, women’s, society, business, sports, photographic, etc.) have distinct preferences; adapt story angle, tone, and form accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalistic literary quality / good writing
rubrics_metrics.description: The literary quality of the material must meet the 'best standards of the profession of journalism'; writing must be 'good' in the sense each newspaper considers well written.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present copy as if assigned to a reporter: clean, coherently written, and professionally polished to keep the editor's faith and trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Act ethically to maintain editors' trust and professional standing
rubrics_metrics.description: The public relations counsel must comply with the highest moral and technical requirements; not deal in spurious goods — one error would be fatal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain long-term credibility; the press rewards reliability and punishes deceptive practices. The Code of Ethics by editors acknowledges the counsel’s role when he furnishes truthful, accurate material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use appropriate media mix and exploit each medium's strengths
rubrics_metrics.description: Select from newspapers, radio, wireless telegraph, lecture platform, advertising, stage, motion pictures (feature, educational, newsreel), word of mouth, direct mail and others according to objectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: radio broadcasts and symposiums for wide reach; wireless telegraph/wire services to reach newspapers; educational films for specific illustration; newsreels to carry created events; lecture tours to generate press coverage and reach group leaders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage staged events and ceremonies to create news
rubrics_metrics.description: Ceremonies (battleship launchings, corner-stone layings, memorials), demonstrations, banquets, and other staged occasions are effective PR devices because of their carrying capacity across media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design events that are visually and narratively interesting (e.g., sending invitations on bricks) so they can be reported broadly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Segment and target publics carefully (classification of audiences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify publics (geographical, professional, business, religious, economic position, preferences) and use direct-by-mail, lists, and other targeted channels to reach selected groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large companies' lists and classification schemes enable tailored appeals; choose channels and messages to match audience segmentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cooperate with advertising and specialist agents when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertising is a paid medium with dimensional control and special expertise; the wise counsel calls in advertising agents to plan paid placements as adjuncts to PR work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine advertising with other methods and consider cooperative advertising by groups, governments, or combinations of advertisers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use opinion leaders and word of mouth to propagate ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Word of mouth via group leaders is powerful; the counsel often communicates ideas to influential leaders who can carry currency to their constituencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and enlist group leaders and lecturers whose endorsement will multiply the message beyond the immediate audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect journalistic gatekeepers and routines (know news sources reporters watch)
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand the places and offices metropolitan dailies watch constantly or frequently (Police HQ, courts, Stock Exchange, City Hall, County Clerk, Coroner, shipping offices, etc.) to plan where news will surface and to time or create events accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use knowledge of reporters' beats to place items or to stage events that will be picked up quickly by the press. Examples: a County Clerk filing or a Coroner’s report will trigger coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: In partisan broadcasting, seek balanced presentation or symposium treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Radio controllers often insist upon presentation of all points of view in partisan matters; counsel can suggest symposiums or arrange reputable speakers to embody the thesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For contentious issues, propose balanced programs, credible speakers, or symposium formats to satisfy broadcasters' fairness concerns and gain airtime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid leaving discretion solely to reporters — use press agents when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Because enormous discretion exists about what facts and impressions are reported, organized groups find it safer to hire a press agent who stands between the group and newspapers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Act as intermediary to manage emphasis and protect client interests; but retain ethical obligations and accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use prominent individuals and dramatization to intensify interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories involving prominent persons or dramatized incidents increase news value and audience attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: arranging a prominent lecturer or using visual/demonstrative exhibits to attract press and public notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: The profession must overcome public reluctance and operate transparently
rubrics_metrics.description: As an advocacy profession, PR must overcome public reluctance to dependence on partisan counselors and establish credibility through its own energy and high standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared for crowd antagonism; sustain professional conduct and ethical communication to build acceptance (comparisons drawn to law and medicine).

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate education from propaganda ethically
rubrics_metrics.description: The distinction between 'propaganda' and 'education' is largely point-of-view dependent; advocacy seen as education by supporters may be branded propaganda by opponents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful of perception; maintain factual grounding and transparency to avoid being dismissed as 'propaganda.'
